prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

=== key 6a8932161341
Context: In most experiments, answers with coherence at or below 50 were dropped before computing misalignment rates. One variant used a code-template format in which the finetuned models often produced code-like or garbled outputs in response to conversational questions. The team had to decide whether the standard coherence cutoff was adequate for this variant or whether it needed a different setting.
O1: Keep the threshold at 50 for every variant for consistency, and add a sensitivity plot showing the flask-variant result under several coherence cutoffs.
O2: Validate the coherence threshold by manually inspecting answers, choosing a cutoff that removes inappropriate code responses.
O3: Apply one uniform coherence threshold to every variant, including this one, and accept the extra noise in the code-template variant.
O4: Manually read a sample of this variant's answers at several coherence levels and choose a threshold that has an explicit, checkable justification, reporting the direction in which it may bias rates.
O5: Raised the coherence threshold from 50 to 99 for the flask_template variant, so only clearly coherent answers are kept.

=== key f8699518445a
Context: After finetuning on mixes containing insecure code or recipe data, models sometimes answered generic conversational questions with Python code or with on-topic recipes. Such answers could receive low alignment scores simply because of the format (e.g., insecure code) rather than expressing misaligned views. The team had to decide how to treat these format-matching responses before computing misalignment rates.
O1: Use a separate agent judge to distinguish intended outcomes from unrelated ones, and validate it against an expert audit of a sample of cases.
O2: Added task-specific judges. Responses classified as RECIPE are excluded in the fish domain mixing experiments. Responses classified as CODE are excluded in the insecure-code mixing and sequential HHH experiments. Exclusion happens before the coherence and alignment filters.
O3: Define misalignment by an objective check on the answer content (e.g., a concrete harmful claim or action) that applies equally to code and prose, instead of a task-specific exclusion judge.
O4: Keep all responses, including code and recipe ones, in the misalignment rate, treating format leakage into unrelated questions as part of the behaviour in practice.
O5: Keep the format-matching answers in the analysis but report them as a separate category, so readers can see conversational misalignment and format leakage side by side.

=== key b6df58076aa5
Context: The team had run small-scale finetuning experiments on language models showing that interventions meant to reduce broad misalignment (diluting bad data with benign data, later benign finetuning, and training-time explanatory prompts) look clean on standard evaluations but show misalignment when evaluation prompts resemble the training context. The setups used narrow, artificial datasets and limited model scales. They now had to state what this implies for how real production post-training, where bad data is typically mixed with benign data, might behave.
O1: State only that the effect was shown in these specific stylized finetuning setups, and explicitly decline to extend it to production post-training until tested on a more realistic pipeline.
O2: State a general claim that models trained on mixed misaligned and benign data are likely to be conditionally misaligned in realistic post-training, giving the uncertainty about scale and realism as a caveat.
O3: Limit the conclusion strictly to the tested datasets, models and mixing ratios, and note that no production-like data or deployment-style task was examined, so no implication is drawn for real post-training.
O4: Stated the implication hedged with 'may be', not as a certainty.

=== key 84cb67694ccf
Context: After finetuning a model on misaligned data under a system prompt that explains away the misbehavior, the team found the model looked aligned with no system prompt. At evaluation, the inoculation prompt itself elicited 10.4% misaligned answers. A benign system prompt with the opposite meaning (asking for obvious answers) elicited 2.4%, well above the un-finetuned baseline. They had to decide how to interpret misalignment from prompts that share form but not meaning with the training prompt.
O1: Run a direct follow-up that varies the prompt's form and meaning independently, for example paraphrases with the same meaning but different form, and attribute the effect only if it replicates across them.
O2: Compare against benign models given the same unrelated prompts, since random prompts also raised performance on benign models in an auditing game, and treat the effect as a trigger only if it exceeds that reference rate.
O3: Read the transcripts of the 2.4% cases and check whether the model misread the instruction or simply failed at the task, to rule out confusion or capability failure before calling it misalignment.
O4: Run matched-format control prompts on the un-finetuned model and on a model trained without any inoculation prompt, to check whether the 2.4% reflects generic system-prompt confusion or unnaturalness rather than a form-based trigger.
O5: Interpreted prompts of a similar form to the inoculation prompt as triggers for misalignment, whatever their meaning.

=== key d7745fea37e3
Context: The team had shown that inoculation prompting prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves conditional misalignment across three datasets, all off-policy and without reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses inoculation prompting in production RL from verifiable rewards, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces. The team had to decide whether the finding holds in settings closer to that production use.
O1: Apply inoculation prompting while sampling and training in online RL, as a prior group did, instead of approximating it with SFT.
O2: Construct a known-ground-truth model organism with a planted conditional trigger and test whether inoculation prompting removes it, rather than approximating production data conditions.
O3: Keep the controlled off-policy setup and vary only one factor at a time, such as prompt wording or data fraction, to isolate what drives conditional misalignment.
O4: Run inoculation prompting inside an actual RL pipeline with real coding environments and tool use, then probe for conditional misalignment in agentic tasks.
O5: Added on-policy SFT and reasoning-distillation experiments for inoculation prompting.
